title: OpenAI Sells Tokens. Palantir Sells the Rails.
subtitle: While Wall Street argued over which model-maker would win, Palantir quietly became the operating system for institutional AI — and its data ontology is the moat the AI trade keeps underestimating.
summary: Palantir builds the rails under institutional AI — the software that turns raw models into operational decisions via its data ontology. Q2 revenue nearly doubled, commercial caught up to government, and the Pentagon made Maven a Program of Record. Here's why the ontology moat matters more than the model wars.

bodyHtml:
While the market spent 2026 arguing about which frontier lab would win — the smartest model, the biggest cluster, the loudest open-weights manifesto — Palantir's Alex Karp kept asking a blunter question. What good is a token if it never changes a decision? He calls token-based AI a "wealth tax" on corporate America. Palantir, meanwhile, sells the rails. If models are the fuel, Palantir built the pipeline.

Here's what Palantir does, in one sentence you can repeat at dinner: it builds the software that helps governments and big companies turn messy data into decisions. Gotham runs defense and intelligence operations. Foundry does the same job for commercial giants. And AIP — the Artificial Intelligence Platform — straps large language models onto both, so organizations can put AI to work on their actual operations instead of just demoing it in a keynote. The customers read like a map of the world's critical infrastructure: intelligence agencies, automakers, airlines, hospitals, energy majors.

The moat is the ontology: Palantir's live map of everything that matters to an organization — contracts, aircraft, shipments, patients, suppliers — and how it all connects. Any lab can ship a smarter model. Very few can plug that model into the real world and make it change an outcome. Every model-maker wants to be the brain. Palantir would rather be the nervous system.

Okay, but does it work? The proof is compounding. Q2 revenue hit $1.935B, up 93% year over year, with U.S. commercial revenue up 149%. Gross margin sits at 84.7%, adjusted free cash flow margin at 63%, and the Rule of 40 — growth plus margin — clocks in at 155, a number most software companies would need a Ouija board to reach. Management raised full-year guidance to $8.15B — the largest raise in the company's history — and the balance sheet is absurdly clean: $9.2B in cash against $211M in debt.

The customer base tells the same story. Palantir now serves 1,049 customers, up 24% year over year. In Q2 alone it closed 220 deals worth at least $1M, 98 worth at least $5M, and 73 worth at least $10M. Its top 20 customers average $124M in trailing revenue, up 67%. And the mix is finally shifting: commercial revenue of $945.4M nearly caught government's $990.0M — a 49/51 split that would've been unthinkable a few years ago, when Palantir was still filed under "defense contractor wearing a tech startup's clothes."

Defense hasn't gone anywhere, though. On August 25, the Pentagon made Maven Smart System — Palantir's AI for targeting and intelligence — a formal Program of Record, with $2.3B sought over five years. Maven platform investment has grown to roughly $13B from $480M in 2024, and William Blair sees the program on track for about $1B in annual recurring revenue. Karp's framing: "Demand for AI sovereignty has now been unleashed. And Palantir is the only company that has demonstrated it can transform tokens into actual economic value." That pitch is landing abroad, too — Stellantis just extended its partnership through 2031, and sovereign-AI demand keeps building.

Now the honest part. The U.S. is 81% of revenue and drove roughly 90% of Q2's growth — a concentration that could sting if the domestic software cycle cools. Palantir doesn't win everything, either: the FAA handed its $875M SMART airspace contract to startup Air Space Intelligence over Palantir and Thales. And the stock took a beating in June's software selloff, falling about 48% from its 52-week high before rallying roughly 40% off the low after earnings. It still trades well below where it peaked.

Zoom out, though, and the thesis is bigger than any quarter. The 2026 AI debate keeps asking which model-maker wins. Palantir's answer: the model is a commodity, and the rails are the business — the operating system under institutional AI, where data, decisions, and dollars actually meet. On CNBC, Karp accused frontier labs of "trying to drug addict us." The pitch is that Palantir is the sober alternative. Whether you own the stock or not, the company has quietly become the infrastructure the AI trade runs on. That's not a narrative. That's a moat.
